channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: Iran fired missiles at three commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz after a one-week truce expired, triggering US retaliatory strikes — on the same day oil settled at pre-war levels and Wall Street hit record highs.
item.description:
The Revolutionary Guard hit two merchant ships on the evening of 6 July and a third — reportedly including a Qatari LNG carrier and a Saudi crude tanker — on Tuesday morning, the biggest day of attacks since the US-Iran memorandum of understanding was signed less than three weeks ago. US Central Command responded with strikes on Iranian air defences, radar and anti-ship missile sites. The escalation collides head-on with the normalisation narrative that had taken hold: Brent traded at USD 72, below pre-war levels, supported by OPEC+ output increases and a US-protected Hormuz corridor; Wall Street closed at record highs on AI and chip momentum; and shipping analysts had just concluded the industry would largely return to its pre-war status quo, with container lines far less Hormuz-dependent than energy tankers.

Industry Impact

For chemical and ACS producers, the attacks are a direct test of the fragile-normalisation thesis flagged in earlier runs: feedstock and freight costs had been the main margin relief of recent weeks, and the IEA has warned buffer stocks are thin. A renewed closure would hit a market with far less spare capacity than in February — supply contingency planning should not be unwound yet.

Lianhe Zaobao | Reuters | Cinco Días | Al Jazeera | Axios | NPR

item.title: ECB Board member Schnabel said falling oil prices do not restore pre-war conditions as core inflation persists, while Panetta warned against repeating the aggressive 2022 hiking cycle in a "Great Reconfiguration".
item.description:
Speaking in Rome, Schnabel pointed to lingering energy-market risks, persistent supply-chain pressures and stubborn core inflation as reasons policymakers cannot declare victory, explicitly noting the peace agreement is fragile — a judgment vindicated within hours by the renewed Hormuz attacks. Panetta, Bank of Italy governor, described the euro-area outlook as fragile and framed the environment as a "Great Reconfiguration" of geopolitics, energy, supply chains and wages that demands scenario-based policy rather than mechanical tightening. He argued a 2022-style maxi hiking cycle would be a mistake because demand is weaker and real rates are already higher. The remarks extend the ESM's warning, covered 6 July, that a combined US-market correction and Middle East relapse could push the euro area into recession in 2027.

Industry Impact

For capital-intensive chemical and construction-linked businesses, the message is higher-for-longer financing costs without the demand destruction of another sharp hiking cycle — a manageable but unspectacular backdrop. The bigger planning variable remains energy-driven input costs, which the ECB itself treats as unresolved; hedging and pricing flexibility matter more than rate speculation.

Der Standard | MarketScreener | Il Sole 24 Ore

item.title: 17.2% of German industrial firms report material shortages — a third in chemicals — while Japan considers a strategic naphtha reserve after Hormuz-driven import collapse forced product halts.
item.description:
Ifo data show shortages rising for a sixth month: 17.2% of German industrial companies affected in June, up from 15.9% in May and just 5.8% in January, with chemicals and electronics worst hit at roughly one in three firms. Automotive rose to 15.7% while rubber and plastics eased to 11.3% — evidence the squeeze is concentrating upstream. In Japan, trade minister Akazawa confirmed the government is studying a naphtha stockpiling system after the de facto Hormuz closure since late February collapsed Middle East imports of the petrochemical feedstock, forcing companies to stop selling some products and simplify packaging. Japan already stockpiles crude and LPG; extending this to naphtha would be a structural admission that chemical feedstocks are now strategic goods, comparable to the EU's critical-raw-materials approach.

Industry Impact

Both signals point the same way: chemical supply chains have not normalised even as headline oil prices have. For ACS producers, upstream shortages mean allocation risk and price volatility in resins, solvents and speciality inputs through H2. Japan's stockpiling debate is worth watching as a template — state-backed feedstock buffers would change competitive dynamics between regions with and without them.

Handelsblatt | The Mainichi

item.title: German manufacturing output rose 0.9% in May — nine times the consensus — led by automotive (+3.6%), while June car registrations jumped 15.7% with hybrids taking a 39% share.
item.description:
Destatis reported May production up 0.9% month-on-month against a 0.1% consensus, though April was revised down to 0.2%. Automotive led with +3.6%, consistent with the order intake surprise (+1.9%) reported a day earlier — Germany's industrial recovery is now visible in both orders and output. On the demand side, KBA registered 296,378 new passenger cars in June, up 15.7% year-on-year: hybrids rose 16.8% to a 39% market share, petrol fell 16.8% to 20.5% and diesel declined to 11.4%. Tesla's Model Y quadrupled registrations (+362%), and Chinese brands continued gaining ground — the same brands whose 10% western-European share is driving Brussels' trade response (see insight 5). The data marks the strongest combined German industrial signal since the Iran war began, though Ifo's material-shortage figures (insight 3) show the supply side has not kept pace.

Industry Impact

Rising German automotive production and double-digit registration growth are direct volume drivers for adhesives, coatings and sealants in Henkel's home market. The powertrain mix shift matters as much as volume: hybrids and EVs carry higher adhesive content per vehicle (battery assembly, lightweighting, thermal management) than the shrinking petrol/diesel segment — a structurally favourable trend if supply bottlenecks don't cap output.

Handelsblatt | Frankfurter Rundschau | Handelsblatt — Tesla

item.title: Chancellor Merz called for coordinated renminbi appreciation to correct China's surplus, while the European Commission signals its "China shock 2.0" response is moving from rhetoric to decisions.
item.description:
Merz's call for a new Plaza Agreement — referencing the 1985 accord that forced yen appreciation — is the sharpest German rhetoric yet on China's trade surplus, though critics argue the surplus reflects weak Chinese domestic demand rather than currency manipulation. It lands as Brussels signals imminent measures against subsidised Chinese EV, solar, battery and steel exports, building on the October 2024 countervailing duties (7.8–35.3%) and the January 2026 minimum-price system for Chinese EV makers. An OECD report gives the hawks ammunition: Chinese companies received three to eight times more government support than OECD peers between 2004 and 2025. The pressure is grounded in market reality — Chinese carmakers' share in 18 western European countries doubled year-on-year to 10% in April, overtaking Japanese brands. Beijing's counter-narrative, and the risk of retaliation against European exporters, remains the unresolved variable.

Industry Impact

An EU-China trade escalation cuts both ways for the chemical industry: protection for European industrial customers (automotive, steel) could stabilise regional demand, but retaliation would threaten European chemical exports to China and raise input costs where Chinese intermediates dominate. Henkel's dual exposure — supplying both European OEMs and Chinese manufacturing — argues for scenario planning rather than betting on either outcome.

Lianhe Zaobao | South China Morning Post | Neue Zürcher Zeitung | SCMP — EV share

item.title: The French government lowered its growth forecast to 0.7% and conceded its 5%-of-GDP deficit target is now "difficult to achieve", with €3 billion in additional cuts under discussion.
item.description:
Finance minister Lescure trimmed the forecast from 0.9% (itself cut from 1% in January), citing a weak start to the year, the budget delay and the Iran war's impact. The figure aligns with INSEE, IMF and OECD; the Banque de France sits lower at 0.5%. The fiscal consequence is immediate: Lescure admitted the 5% deficit target is at risk, budget minister Amiel flagged an extra €3 billion of cuts or freezes on top of €6 billion already planned, and the finance ministry sees a potential €2 billion local-government overshoot. All of this feeds the 2027 budget due in September — which Lescure wants to bring the deficit below 5% — in a political environment reshaped by the Le Pen ruling (insight 7). France's trajectory contrasts with Germany's improving data (insight 4), widening the eurozone's internal growth gap.

Industry Impact

France is Europe's second-largest construction and manufacturing market; sub-1% growth plus fiscal tightening means soft demand for construction chemicals and industrial adhesives into 2027. Public-investment cuts would hit infrastructure-linked volumes first. The France-Germany divergence suggests reweighting European demand assumptions toward the German rebound rather than a broad eurozone recovery.

Les Echos | Le Figaro | Bloomberg

item.title: The Paris appeal court upheld Le Pen's EU-funds conviction but cut her election ban to 15 months, largely served since March 2025 — she immediately declared she is still standing for president.
item.description:
The court confirmed the fictitious-employment conviction, imposing a three-year sentence (two suspended), one year under an electronic ankle tag and a €100,000 fine, while reducing the ineligibility period from five years to 15 months. Because the first-instance ban has been provisionally enforced since late March 2025, it is considered largely served — technically reopening her path to the April 2027 election. Le Pen declared she remains a candidate, though she had previously said she would not run while wearing an ankle tag, leaving real ambiguity about whether she or protégé Jordan Bardella carries the National Rally banner. Polls give RN a strong chance of winning; centrist hopefuls, including Édouard Philippe, are positioning on fiscal restraint to block them. The ruling lands as the government cuts growth forecasts and drafts an austerity budget (insight 6) — a volatile combination.

Industry Impact

A plausible RN path to the Élysée in April 2027 is now a base-case scenario for markets, not a tail risk. For industry, the questions are RN's stance on EU integration, energy policy and labour costs in Europe's second economy. Expect elevated French political-risk premia and hesitant corporate investment through the campaign — reinforcing the soft French demand outlook.

Handelsblatt | Politico Europe | CNN | Euronews

item.title: The World Bank's "Rebalancing Growth" update keeps China's 2026 forecast at 4.4%, crediting high-tech investment and exports while flagging property adjustment, cautious consumers and a 4.3% 2027 outlook.
item.description:
The update, released in Beijing on 7 July, holds the 2026 projection unchanged from December and notes growth could exceed it. High-tech investment rose 4.5% year-on-year in January–May on robust AI demand, and policy support plus energy buffers offset weaker domestic demand in Q2 — China weathered the Gulf energy shock through reserves and reduced imports. The structural message is less comfortable: the property sector continues adjusting to lower housing demand, consumption rebalancing is slow, and growth eases to 4.3% in 2027. The Bank urges stronger social safety nets and support for workers in the low-carbon transition. The report indirectly validates both sides of the European debate (insight 5): China's export strength is real, and so is the domestic-demand weakness that critics say drives the surplus.

Industry Impact

For chemical suppliers, the composition of China's growth matters more than the headline: high-tech manufacturing and AI-linked electronics are expanding — adhesive-intensive segments — while property-linked construction chemicals face a continued structural drag. The 15th Five-Year Plan's urban renewal agenda may partially offset the housing decline; positioning should follow the investment mix, not the GDP number.

Global Times | Xinhua | World Bank

item.title: Twenty-two Democratic AGs called proposed 12.5% tariffs on 59 countries and the EU unlawful, while KPMG finds 42% of Canadian manufacturers have moved or plan to move production to the US.
item.description:
The attorneys general argue the forced-labour-based tariffs are a pretext to replace levies invalidated by the Supreme Court and will extend the economic damage of earlier rounds — signalling a new legal fight if the administration proceeds. The real-economy effect is already visible north of the border: KPMG's survey of 275 Canadian manufacturers finds 42% have relocated or are considering relocating production to the US, 77% of those within two years; 57% have paused or cut capital projects and 42% scaled back R&D. Meanwhile, French analysis argues the trade war has produced reorganisation rather than deglobalisation — US-China flows contracted sharply since 2025's "Liberation Day", but trade rerouted through third countries. Tariff uncertainty, not tariffs themselves, is doing the investment damage.

Industry Impact

Production migration toward the US pulls adhesive and coating demand with it — regional supply footprints need to follow customers, not countries. For a European supplier, the KPMG numbers underline the case for US manufacturing capacity, while the AGs' challenge and Supreme Court precedent mean tariff levels remain litigable and unstable — arguing against irreversible supply-chain commitments based on current rates.

Reuters | AP | The Globe and Mail | Challenges

item.title: Trump said he expects to host Xi Jinping in the US around 24 September; the Dow closed above 53,000 for the first time as investors priced in trade détente.
item.description:
The announcement, made 6 July, sets the first Trump-Xi summit of the current escalation cycle and gives both sides a deadline to assemble deliverables. Markets treated it as a de-escalation signal: the Dow recovered from an intraday 251-point drop to a record close above 53,000, with all four major indices higher. The timing is notable — it follows the proposed 59-country tariff round (insight 9) and Europe's hardening stance (insight 5), positioning Washington to negotiate bilaterally while Brussels weighs its own measures. Previous Trump-Xi meetings produced tactical pauses rather than structural resolution; the pattern to watch is whether a September deal trades tariff relief for Chinese purchase commitments, and where that leaves the EU.

Industry Impact

A US-China accommodation in September would ease the tariff overhang on globally traded chemical inputs and electronics supply chains — positive for volumes. The risk case: a bilateral US-China deal that excludes Europe would leave EU exporters facing Chinese overcapacity redirected from the US market. Contingency planning for both outcomes should precede the summit.

Commercial Times

item.title: At the NATO summit, Trump said a Ukraine agreement is nearer than assumed after calls with Putin and talks with Zelensky, who is expected to request additional air-defence systems.
item.description:
Trump told reporters he is in parallel talks with Moscow and Kyiv and believes Putin wants to end the war; Zelensky, attending the Ankara summit, also seeks an end and will press for air-defence reinforcement. This continues the momentum reported on 6 July, when a draft Ankara Declaration reportedly included €70 billion for Ukraine (with Italy blocking parts) and all 32 allies reached the 2% GDP spending floor. The optimism now coexists with maximum pressure on Russia — sanctions on chemical-weapons institutes, fuel shortages across nearly all Russian regions from Ukrainian drone strikes — and with no confirmed ceasefire mechanism. Expert consensus remains that verification and territorial questions, not intent declarations, are the binding constraints.

Industry Impact

A credible settlement would unlock the largest European reconstruction programme since 1945 — cement, insulation, sealants, adhesives and coatings demand measured in years — and normalise regional energy and logistics costs. The discipline: previous "close" moments have not converted. Treat reconstruction as upside scenario, not plannable demand, until a ceasefire mechanism exists.

Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | The Economic Times

item.title: Rutte demanded a defence-industry "revolution" and unveiled USD 12 billion in deals — up to 10 Saab GlobalEyes, five Northrop Tritons, an A400M fleet — while Germany plans 500 fighter-bomber drones by 2029.
item.description:
At the Ankara summit, NATO chose Saab's GlobalEye (built on Bombardier 6500 jets) to replace its aging Boeing E-3 fleet — a European solution over the US E-7 Wedgetail, despite American pressure; 11 countries including Canada join the ~USD 5 billion procurement. Denmark, Finland, Germany and Norway will buy up to five MQ-4C Triton surveillance drones (USD 2.7 billion), and a new multinational A400M transport project was launched. Rutte called for "the hum of the machines to become a roar": long-term orders, less bureaucracy, more industry risk-taking, with alliance artillery-shell output to reach four million annually by 2027. Germany separately plans up to 500 fighter-bomber drones (500 kg payload, 1,000+ km range) by 2029 and awarded AeroVironment the LARUS reconnaissance programme — a multi-billion pipeline for German industry.

Industry Impact

Defence is becoming a durable European industrial demand pillar. Aerospace and defence platforms are intensive users of structural adhesives, composites bonding, sealants and specialty coatings; drone mass-production at automotive-like volumes is a new segment with different qualification cycles. The European-preference pattern (Saab over Boeing) suggests EU-based suppliers will be favoured in the value chain.

Süddeutsche Zeitung | Financial Post | CBC | Handelsblatt | Breaking Defense

item.title: The ISM Manufacturing PMI registered 53.3% in June — a sixth straight month of expansion — with the Prices Index down 9.1 points to 73% and employment nearing growth at 49.7%.
item.description:
The June reading confirms US manufacturing's post-war expansion has staying power, in contrast to the services PMI, which eased to 54.0 as war-driven order front-loading faded (reported 6 July). The sharp drop in the Prices Index — from 82.1 to 73% — is the most consequential detail: input-cost pressure that had been fuelled by the energy shock and tariff rounds is finally decelerating, though 73% still signals rising prices, just more slowly. The Employment Index at 49.7% approaches expansion after months of contraction, consistent with the cooling-but-stable labour market (unemployment 4.2%). Benchmarked against Europe: the US expansion contrasts with the UK construction PMI stuck at 38.4 and Germany's recovery that is real but supply-constrained (insight 3) — the US remains the strongest large industrial economy this cycle.

Industry Impact

Six months of expanding US factory activity supports industrial adhesives and surface-treatment volumes in Henkel's largest single market, and easing input-price pressure helps margin recovery. Combined with Canadian production migration southward (insight 9), the data reinforces the US as the demand-growth pole of the Atlantic economy — with tariff policy the main downside risk to that trajectory.

ISM

item.title: UK chemical output grew just 0.1% in Q1, still below its 2023 baseline, while European producers — Nouryon, CABB, Lanxess, Ineos — exploit a war-driven window to refinance debt.
item.description:
The Chemical Industries Association's quarterly survey confirms UK chemicals remain in structural stagnation: 0.1% growth within manufacturing, below the 2023 baseline, mirroring the continent-wide pattern of high energy costs and weak demand. The counterintuitive bright spot is financial: Lazard reports European chemical makers are using a brief post-Iran-war window to refinance, as supply disruptions lifted sentiment for European producers — less feedstock-exposed than Asian rivals — while credit-market liquidity fuels investor appetite. Nouryon, CABB, Lanxess and Ineos have all extended maturities. This is balance-sheet repair, not recovery: the ICC/KPMG "decade of uncertainty" diagnosis covered on 6 July still stands, and the refinancing window depends on exactly the fragile normalisation the Hormuz attacks (insight 1) now threaten.

Industry Impact

Competitors strengthening balance sheets means the European consolidation phase continues on financial rather than operational logic — expect asset disposals and portfolio reshuffling among refinanced players. For Henkel, stronger-financed upstream suppliers reduce near-term supply-security risk but the underlying European cost disadvantage versus the US and Middle East is unchanged; the UK data is the honest baseline.

Chemical Industries Association | Financial Post

item.title: China projects humanoid robot output above 100,000 units in 2026; robotics enterprise revenue passed CNY 90 billion (+26.9%) in five months, and AI industries exceeded CNY 1 trillion in 2025.
item.description:
MIIT's announcement ahead of the World AI Conference (17–20 July, Shanghai) quantifies China's lead in embodied AI: humanoid production above 100,000 units this year, AI penetration past 30% of larger industrial enterprises, and a national AI fund channelling capital into the sector. Supporting data reinforce the scale: robotics enterprise turnover rose 26.9% to over CNY 90 billion January–May, and the NDRC puts 2025 AI-industry scale above CNY 1 trillion. Benchmarked internationally, no other economy is producing humanoids at five-figure volumes; Western deployments remain pilot-stage. The World Bank's 4.4% forecast (insight 8) explicitly credits this high-tech investment as China's growth engine while property adjusts — robotics is the designated successor industry, echoing the EV playbook that produced today's European trade tensions (insight 5).

Industry Impact

Humanoid and industrial robot manufacturing is an emerging adhesives and coatings segment — precision bonding, lightweight composites, thermal-interface materials — with China as the volume centre. The strategic echo matters: if robotics follows the EV trajectory, expect Chinese export dominance and Western trade defence within three to five years. Early design-in positions with Chinese robot OEMs are the offensive play; monitoring EU response is the defensive one.

Xinhua | China Daily | Xhby.net | Chinatimes
